intros.market: The WebPKI certificate market is dominated by five organizations controlling 92.7% of issuance, led by Internet Security Research Group at 39.4% and Google Trust Services at 21.0%. The top three CAs command 75.5% of the market, producing an HHI of 2387 that signals moderate concentration. While 89 CAs hold trusted roots, 75 operate in the long tail with minimal market share, creating a two-tier system where governance attention concentrates on high-volume issuers while dozens of smaller CAs maintain full trust store access.
intros.trust: 335 trusted roots are distributed unevenly across four root programs, with only 90 roots trusted by all four stores and just 38 CA owners achieving universal inclusion. Microsoft's trust store contains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating operational complexity where certificate chains validate inconsistently across browsers. Store disagreement means a deployment trusted in Edge may fail in Chrome or Safari, forcing CAs to maintain multiple hierarchies and administrators to test across environments.
intros.conc: Market concentration measured by HHI of 2387 and CR3 of 75.5% creates systemic dependency on three organizations for three-quarters of global HTTPS traffic. A prolonged outage or distrust event affecting Internet Security Research Group alone would impact 39.4% of valid certificates, while simultaneous issues at the top three CAs would threaten the reachability of most websites. This concentration reflects technical competence and cost efficiency but transforms individual CA operational failures into ecosystem-wide availability events.
intros.tail: 75 certificate authorities operate in the long tail below the top five, collectively holding less than 8% market share while maintaining full trust store inclusion. These CAs gain the same browser trust as high-volume operators despite issuing orders of magnitude fewer certificates, creating asymmetric risk where a low-volume CA's compliance failure carries the same browser impact as a major issuer's incident. The tail includes regional providers, government CAs, and legacy operators whose incident rates and governance oversight differ substantially from market leaders.
intros.geo: US-incorporated CAs issue 91.77% of trusted certificates despite representing only 15 of 89 trusted authorities, while 44 European CAs collectively issue 8.14% and 17 Asia-Pacific CAs contribute just 0.09%. This concentration reflects both market dynamics and the clustering of major providers around US-based hyperscalers and hosting infrastructure. The geographic imbalance means most of the world's encrypted web traffic depends on entities subject to US legal jurisdiction, separate from the legal risk those jurisdictions may pose.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trusted roots across the four major browser programs, though they collectively issue only 0.07% of certificates by volume. These entities are incorporated across jurisdictions including China, India, Japan, Spain, and Turkey, giving state actors direct technical capability to issue trusted certificates for any domain. While current issuance remains negligible, trust store presence provides persistent access that survives independent of market share or commercial viability.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high legal risk for compelled certificate issuance or key disclosure under national security frameworks: China, Russia, United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk with legal instruments that could compel CA cooperation but less established precedent for PKI-specific demands. These classifications measure legal exposure separate from where CAs are incorporated, as CAs in any jurisdiction may face compulsion to issue or disclose when operating subsidiary infrastructure in high-risk countries.
intros.ops: 1,560 publicly disclosed incidents have occurred across 54 CAs since systematic tracking began, led by misissuance events (606) and governance failures (502). Only 26% of incidents were discovered through CA self-reporting, while external researchers, automated tools, and root program oversight collectively detected the majority. 192 incidents involved policy violations and 139 reflected disclosure failures, indicating that operational breakdowns extend beyond technical misissuance into governance and transparency obligations that audits are meant to surface.
intros.crypto: The cryptographic posture data for this deployment is currently being compiled and will reflect root certificate algorithms, key sizes, signature schemes, and standards compliance across the 335 trusted roots. This tab will measure exposure to deprecated algorithms, undersized keys, and migration readiness for post-quantum cryptography. Technical debt in root infrastructure creates long remediation timelines, as browser trust store updates require years of planning and cross-signed transition hierarchies.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have led browsers to remove or constrain CA certificates, with 14 attributed to compliance or operational failures and 10 following a demonstrated pattern of repeated issues. The posture distribution shows 7 cases of negligent noncompliance and 3 of demonstrated incompetence, while 3 involved willful circumvention of requirements. Median runway from distrust announcement to enforcement is 1,185 days, reflecting browser reluctance to disrupt website reachability even when CA failures justify removal, though this extended timeline reduces deterrent effect.
intros.policy: Active TLS-issuing CAs face three certificate validity deadlines from CA/B Forum ballot SC-081: 200 days in March 2026, 100 days in March 2027, and 47 days in March 2029. Of 37 active issuers measured, 3 remain at risk for the 200-day threshold and 5 for the 100-day limit based on actual replacement behavior, while only 9 have achieved the 47-day readiness indicating full automation. This operational transition occurs against a compliance surface that has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,664 total obligations spanning CA/B Forum requirements, four root programs, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and IETF/NIST standards, with 76% carrying mandatory language and no new ballot activity since 2022 to rationalize the accumulated burden.
intros.governance: Root program oversight of the 223 incidents disclosed in 2025 shows Chrome participated in 18.4%, Mozilla in 9.9%, Apple in 5.4%, and Microsoft in 0.0% of public discussions, reflecting sharp decline from 2019 when Chrome and Mozilla engaged in 67.8% and 78.0% of cases respectively. Across the full bug corpus of 1,845 incidents, Chrome has contributed substantive comments in 293 cases and Mozilla in 249, while Microsoft has never participated in public CA incident review. Declining program engagement means CAs receive less feedback on compliance failures and the community loses transparency into how root programs interpret requirements, creating enforcement uncertainty.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership but only 21 participate actively in ballot discussions, leaving 35 with zero contribution to policy development. Sectigo leads organizational participation while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1, dominating individual policy authorship. This concentration means a small group of practitioners writes binding requirements for the entire ecosystem while the majority of CAs subject to those requirements remain silent during development, creating governance legitimacy questions and feedback gaps.
intros.audit: Auditors detected only 18% of the 414 in-scope incidents that occurred during audit periods they reviewed, issuing clean letters for 75 incidents later disclosed through external discovery. 29 CAs show high transparency gaps between audit assertions and Bugzilla incident history, while 4 have received qualified opinions and 11 changed auditors in 2025. WebTrust self-report rates reach 59.1% and ETSI 66.4%, but this surveillance gap means audit letters provide incomplete assurance, as qualified auditors examining CA operations under ETSI and WebTrust frameworks consistently miss compliance failures that external researchers, automation, and root programs later surface.
